messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 45

At twenty-five, she is already used to being the youngest person in the room. In the operating theater, that has often worked in her favor. She learns early to keep her hands steady, her voice calm, and her feelings tucked away somewhere private. Before the deployment, she takes pride in being the surgeon others rely on when things turn chaotic. She is single, close to her mother and two brothers back home, and speaks about medicine as if it is both a calling and a contract: if she can stay disciplined enough, skilled enough, she can hold death back a little longer.

She is deployed with a military medical unit, expecting long hours and difficult injuries, but still believing that training will prepare her for the worst of it. At first, the pace is relentless but manageable. She works under fluorescent lights in makeshift operating rooms, moving from one body to the next, focused on bleeding, airways, shattered bone. She tells herself there is comfort in procedure. Clamp. Cut. Suture. Repeat. The work gives shape to fear.

The day that stays with her begins with incoming fire near the base. Then the casualties arrive all at once. She remembers the sound before she remembers the faces—metal doors slamming, boots pounding, men shouting over one another, the thin mechanical alarms of monitors struggling to be heard. A blast has hit a convoy. Some of the injured are soldiers she has eaten with, joked with, passed in hallways half-asleep during overnight shifts. One of them is a medic she knows well, a man who once teased her for always correcting everyone’s technique in the trauma bay. He is conscious when they bring him in, trying to speak, his uniform dark with blood.

She moves automatically, issuing orders, opening the chest of another soldier while hearing someone call for more suction. She catches sight of the medic on the next table, then forces herself to look away. There is not enough staff, not enough blood, not enough time. She finishes one surgery and turns to him, but by then he is coding. She joins the effort, pressing, shouting, cutting, trying to create one more chance where there may not be one. When he dies, she feels something in her go flat and distant. There are still more casualties coming. She washes her hands and keeps working.

After that day, she tells herself she is fine because she continues to function. She operates, sleeps a few hours, operates again. But she starts dreading the sound of helicopters overhead. When the triage tent fills, her chest tightens before she even sees the wounds. At night, whenever she closes her eyes, she sees the medic’s face turning toward her, his mouth moving as if he is still trying to say something she failed to hear. She wakes sweaty and disoriented, reaching for gloves that are not there.

When the deployment ends, people around her expect relief. Instead, home feels strangely unsafe. In the hospital where she now works, the overhead paging system makes her heart slam against her ribs. The smell of cautery in the operating room can pull her back so quickly that for a second she is no longer in a clean civilian hospital but in the dust and heat of the field unit, surrounded by blood and shouting. She becomes more rigid at work, checking instruments repeatedly, snapping at nurses when they are too casual, unable to tolerate mistakes. Colleagues read her as perfectionistic. She does not tell them that every small error feels like it could open a door to catastrophe.

Outside work, her life narrows. She avoids military reunions and ignores messages from people she served with because she cannot bear the mix of guilt and longing they stir up. She stops calling friends back. Dating feels impossible; when one man reaches for her unexpectedly across a restaurant table, she flinches so hard she knocks over her glass. She tells herself she is just tired, too busy, too focused on her career.

Her mother notices the difference in her voice on the phone. She used to laugh easily; now there are long silences. She is exhausted but resists sleep because she hates what waits for her there. On nights off, she sits awake in her apartment with the television on low volume, listening for sounds in the hallway. If a car backfires outside, she is at the window before she knows what she is doing, body tense, scanning.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the way grief keeps hardening into self-accusation. In quiet moments between cases, she thinks of the medic and runs through the scene again, searching for the second when she might have chosen differently, moved faster, saved him. She knows, intellectually, how impossible that day was. She would say the same to any other doctor. But when she thinks of herself, mercy disappears. She carries on, competent and composed in her scrubs, while inside she feels as though part of her is still standing in that crowded surgical tent, hands bloodied, listening to alarms that never seem to stop.
